title: Anastrozole · daily hormone therapy
schedule_summary: Take anastrozole once daily continuously. There is no planned week off. The treatment setting determines the intended duration.
purpose: After early breast cancer treatment, endocrine therapy reduces the risk of recurrence. In advanced disease, the aim is to control cancer and symptoms. Your setting determines the duration and follow-up.

agents.mechanism: Reduces the oestrogen available to stimulate cancer cells
agents.explanation: After menopause, much of the body’s oestrogen is made when aromatase converts other hormones in fat and other tissues. Blocking that enzyme lowers oestrogen signalling in hormone-sensitive breast cancer. It does not reliably switch off functioning ovaries: ovarian suppression, if needed, must be prescribed and checked separately.
agents.watch: Tell the team if joint pain, hot flushes, vaginal dryness or sleep disturbance affects daily life. Bone thinning may cause no early symptoms, so keep the agreed bone-health reviews.
risks: Joint and muscle pain or stiffness
Hot flushes, sleep disturbance and fatigue
Uncommon liver abnormalities or serious allergic reactions

sections.title: A continuous daily medicine
sections.text: Choose a consistent daily routine. There is no chemotherapy-style rest week or automatic restart date.

sections.title: Support joint symptoms
sections.text: Discuss safe physical activity, strength work and symptom treatment. Report symptoms early so the team can consider support or a planned switch instead of you stopping without advice.

sections.title: Keep the bone-health plan
sections.text: Ask when the baseline DXA result will be reviewed and when the next assessment is due. Calcium, vitamin D and bone medicines depend on diet, deficiency and fracture risk.

sections.title: If periods return
sections.text: Tell the oncology team about bleeding or return of periods, particularly after chemotherapy or if menopause was uncertain. Do not assume ovarian suppression is part of this monotherapy card.

evidence.title: ATAC: anastrozole as initial adjuvant therapy
evidence.population: 6,241 postmenopausal women randomized to anastrozole 1 mg or tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 5 years; hormone-receptor-positive subgroup 5,216.
evidence.interpretation: HR-positive subgroup: DFS HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.78–0.95); time-to-recurrence HR 0.79 (0.70–0.89). Absolute recurrence difference favouring anastrozole was 4.3 percentage points at 10 years.
evidence.limitations: Overall mortality did not differ significantly (HR 0.95,95% CI 0.84–1.06). Fractures were more frequent during active anastrozole treatment. These figures describe postmenopausal adjuvant treatment and must not be used as metastatic prognosis or evidence for AI monotherapy with functioning ovaries.

teachback: What is your treatment schedule, which checks apply to your setting, and who books and reviews them?
consent_support: A functioning premenopausal ovarian state is not compatible with AI monotherapy. Severe hepatic impairment is not recommended by NCCP; moderate impairment requires caution. Confirm menopausal status rather than assuming that absent periods after chemotherapy mean permanent menopause. Any ovarian-suppression treatment must have its own prescribed schedule.

support.title: Symptoms and daily life
support.text: Tell the team if joint pain, hot flushes, vaginal dryness or sleep disturbance affects daily life. Bone thinning may cause no early symptoms, so keep the agreed bone-health reviews.

support.title: Support medicines
support.text: No routine antiemetic, steroid premedication or G-CSF is required by this endocrine monotherapy. Ask for individual symptom support.

support.title: Tests and appointments
support.text: Ask who books each check, when it is due and who reviews it. Tell the team if an expected appointment has not arrived.

chapters.title: The exact treatment being discussed
chapters.intro: After early breast cancer treatment, endocrine therapy reduces the risk of recurrence. In advanced disease, the aim is to control cancer and symptoms. Your setting determines the duration and follow-up.

items.title: Who this card covers
items.text: Postmenopausal hormone-sensitive breast cancer in the NCCP adjuvant, switch-after-tamoxifen or advanced settings. The exact receptor and prior-treatment criteria remain a prescribing decision.

items.title: Dose and administration
items.text: 1 mg orally once daily. Swallow with water, with or without food. Do not replace a missed or vomited dose; resume the next scheduled dose.

items.title: Duration and decision points
items.text: In early breast cancer, the standard source course is five years of adjuvant endocrine treatment, including any planned switch from tamoxifen. A later extension decision depends on recurrence risk, tolerance and bone health. Advanced treatment continues according to benefit.

items.title: Individual safety
items.text: A functioning premenopausal ovarian state is not compatible with AI monotherapy. Severe hepatic impairment is not recommended by NCCP; moderate impairment requires caution.

chapters.title: Checks throughout treatment
chapters.intro: Baseline, ongoing safety checks and cancer scans have different purposes.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: FBC, renal and liver profile. Confirm menopause; hormone tests may be needed if it is uncertain. Assess fracture risk and baseline bone density, particularly for adjuvant AI treatment. The NICE adjuvant baseline-DXA recommendation has an exception for patients already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Assess symptoms, adherence and bone health at reviews. Repeat lipids and other blood tests when clinically indicated. Bone-density timing follows baseline results and fracture risk.

items.title: Heart checks
items.text: There is no routine ECG or echo schedule for anastrozole alone. Review cardiovascular risk factors and investigate cardiac symptoms when indicated.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: Offer baseline DXA when starting an adjuvant aromatase inhibitor if not already receiving adjuvant bisphosphonates; assess fracture risk and relevant previous results. Under the 2025 joint guidance, patients with a T-score above −2.0 and no additional risk factors generally have risk and bone density reassessed every one to two years. Patients on bone-protective treatment generally have BMD reassessed about every two years. Fracture, substantial bone loss or a change in risk can require earlier review. The clinician selects the interval and any bone treatment; these are not automatic yearly scans for everyone.

chapters.title: Your setting changes the pathway
chapters.intro: Choose the pathway that your team has confirmed; these are not all extra treatments you must have.

items.title: Early-breast follow-up
items.text: After curative treatment, annual mammography is generally used for remaining breast tissue: both breasts after conservation or the opposite breast after unilateral mastectomy. The mastectomy side is not routinely mammographed. Routine CT, bone scans and tumour markers are not recommended for asymptomatic early-breast surveillance. New symptoms need assessment between appointments.

items.title: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy
items.text: In an early-breast pathway, chemotherapy, if indicated, precedes endocrine treatment. Surgery and its pathology guide adjuvant choices. Postoperative radiotherapy is usually delivered after recovery and any adjuvant chemotherapy; aromatase inhibitors may overlap radiotherapy under the agreed plan. Tamoxifen timing around radiotherapy is agreed by the treating teams. None of these additional treatments is automatically required by an endocrine prescription.

items.title: Advanced-disease scans
items.text: For advanced breast cancer, response assessment is generally every two to four months, adapted to disease pace, sites, symptoms and treatment. Indolent disease may be reviewed less often; new symptoms can prompt earlier scans. The team chooses the imaging method; this is not a universal three-month CT chest/abdomen/pelvis order.

items.title: Tumour markers
items.text: Tumour markers may supplement imaging and clinical assessment in advanced disease if they are informative, especially if elevated at baseline. They do not replace scans, and a marker change alone should not determine treatment failure. There is no universal fixed marker timetable.

items.title: Menopause, pregnancy and contraception
items.text: Confirm menopausal status rather than assuming that absent periods after chemotherapy mean permanent menopause. Any ovarian-suppression treatment must have its own prescribed schedule.

questions.q: Do I need a port or home pump?
questions.a: No port or home infusion pump is needed for this medicine itself. Any separately prescribed medicine has its own access requirements.
